claim: In July 2023, two preprints claimed that a material called LK-99 was a superconductor at room temperature, a discovery that would transform electronics. Within weeks, other labs tried to reproduce the result (Garisto, 2023)
source_url: https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-023-02585-7 (Nature 620, 705-706; standfirst and reference list read, body paywalled); https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-023-02481-0 (Nature 620, 253; standfirst read, body paywalled); arXiv 2307.12008 and 2307.12037 (API read)
correction: RESOLVED with edits. Two arXiv preprints on LK-99 were posted on 22 July 2023 (2307.12008, 2307.12037; API timestamps 07:51 and 10:11 UTC). Nature news of 4 Aug 2023 (Garisto): the claim "prompted a slew of replication efforts by scientists and amateurs alike", and initial efforts "have come up short". Nature news of 16 Aug 2023 (Garisto): researchers "seem to have solved the puzzle"; evidence that "the material is not a superconductor". Nature bodies are paywalled: only standfirsts were read. "A discovery that would transform electronics" is not in either standfirst. REPLACEMENT: "In July 2023, two preprints claimed that a material called LK-99 was a superconductor at room temperature and ordinary pressure, which would be a major advance. Within weeks, labs around the world tried to reproduce the result, and by mid-August the evidence pointed away from superconductivity (Garisto, 2023a, 2023b)." Add reference 2023a: Garisto, D. (2023, August 4). Claimed superconductor LK-99 is an online sensation, but replication efforts fall short. *Nature, 620*(7973), 253. https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-023-02481-0. Reference 2023b: Garisto, D. (2023). LK-99 isn't a superconductor: How science sleuths solved the mystery. *Nature, 620*(7975), 705-706. https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-023-02585-7 (published 16 August 2023).

claim: GRADE rates certainty of a body of evidence; randomized trials start high, observational studies start low; it moves the rating down for risk of bias, inconsistent results, indirect evidence, imprecise estimates and signs of unpublished unfavorable studies; up for very large effects
source_url: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2335261/ (Guyatt et al., 2008, full text read); https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclinepi.2010.07.015 (Balshem et al., 2011, record only)

Guyatt et al. 2008 (BMJ 336:924-926): evidence from randomised trials begins as high quality, confidence may be decreased for "Study limitations, Inconsistency of results, Indirectness of evidence, Imprecision, Reporting bias"; observational studies start "low", and grading up "may be warranted if the magnitude of the treatment effect is very large ..., if there is evidence of a dose-response relation or if all plausible biases would decrease the magnitude of an apparent treatment effect"; four levels: high, moderate, low, very low. Terminology: the 2008 paper says "quality" of evidence; later GRADE papers say "certainty". REPLACEMENT (last sentence): "It can move the rating up, for example when an effect is very large or when there is a dose-response pattern (Guyatt et al., 2008). Early GRADE papers called the rating 'quality' of evidence; later ones say 'certainty'." Delete [VERIFY]. Optional added reference: Balshem, H., et al. (2011). GRADE guidelines: 3.
